metaData.title: Build agents， not pipelines
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: This article argues that when building LLM-powered programs, agents are generally superior to pipelines due to their flexibility, intelligence, and ease of context-gathering, despite being less predictable.
metaData.summary: The article presents a clear dichotomy for using LLMs in software: pipelines, where control flow is defined in code, and agents, where the LLM manages control flow using tools. It argues that while pipelines offer predictability and are suitable for strict context size or cost constraints, agents are smarter and more flexible, especially for complex tasks like coding. The author details how context-gathering is far easier for agents, as they can fetch information on demand, whereas pipelines require complex upfront assembly (e.g., RAG), which often fails. The article also discusses trade-offs in multi-model pipelines, safety, and legibility, concluding that agents are more future-proof. Practical guidelines are provided, recommending agents when in doubt, as they are easier to build and more likely to solve the actual problem.

mainPoints.point: Agents are smarter and more flexible than pipelines for complex tasks.
mainPoints.explanation: Agents can loop and gather information as needed, handling much harder problems. Pipelines are more predictable but limited by their fixed control flow and context.

mainPoints.point: Context-gathering is significantly easier with agents than with pipelines.
mainPoints.explanation: Agents can fetch data on demand using tools like 'grep' and 'read file'. Pipelines require complex upfront assembly (e.g., RAG), which often fails to surface the precise information needed.

mainPoints.point: Pipelines are preferable when strict control over cost, latency, or context size is required.
mainPoints.explanation: Pipelines offer predictable performance and are necessary for local models with limited context windows. Agents can be unpredictable in cost and latency.

mainPoints.point: Agents are more future-proof as they benefit more from LLM improvements.
mainPoints.explanation: Newer models are explicitly built to be better agents, and agentic systems delegate more to the LLM, allowing them to leverage these improvements more effectively than pipelines.

keyQuotes: Pipelines are more predictable, but agents are more flexible.
The context-gathering stage is far more delicate for pipelines than for agents.
I am aware of several AI projects that have migrated from pipelines to agents in the last year, but none that have gone the other way around.

relatedArticles.title: Building Claude Code with Boris Cherny
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Boris Cherny, creator of Claude Code, discusses his 100% AI-driven workflow, Anthropic's unique engineering culture, and why software engineers are transitioning from 'scribes' to 'authors' in the AI era.

relatedArticles.title: AI makes weak engineers less harmful
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: AI coding assistants like Claude Code significantly reduce the negative impact of weak engineers by raising the floor of their output, transforming them from net-negative contributors into functional, albeit limited, collaborators.

relatedArticles.title: Engineers do get promoted for writing simple code
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article challenges the cynical belief that overcomplicating code leads to promotions, arguing instead that writing simple, maintainable code is the most effective path to career advancement because it prioritizes shipping results.

relatedArticles.title: Why I don't like the "staff engineer archetypes"
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article argues that Will Larson's popular 'staff engineer archetypes' are a poor practical goal for engineers, advocating instead for building trust and usefulness to the company organically.

relatedArticles.title: Harness design for long-running application development
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article explores Anthropic's multi-agent harness design (Planner, Generator, Evaluator) for long-running autonomous coding, detailing how to overcome context anxiety and self-evaluation bias to build complex full-stack applications.

relatedArticles.title: How Claude Code works in large codebases: Best practices and where to start | Claude
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article provides a comprehensive guide on deploying Claude Code in large codebases, emphasizing that success depends more on the 'harness' of configuration layers (CLAUDE.md, hooks, skills, plugins, LSP, MCP) than on the model alone, and outlines proven patterns for making codebases navigable, maintaining configurations, and assigning organizational ownership.

relatedArticles.title: Andrej Karpathy on Code Agents， AutoResearch， and the Loopy Era of AI
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Andrej Karpathy explores the paradigm shift from manual programming to agent orchestration, the automation of AI research, and the profound implications for software engineering and education.

relatedArticles.title: Martin Fowler & Kent Beck: Frameworks for reinventing software， again and again
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Software legends Martin Fowler and Kent Beck discuss how AI redefines software engineering, emphasizing that core practices like TDD and modularity remain essential for human-AI collaboration.

relatedArticles.title: How I use LLMs as a staff engineer in 2026
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: A staff engineer details how AI agents have evolved from occasional tools to core workflow components, now handling most code changes and bug investigations under light human supervision.

relatedArticles.title: Programming (with AI agents) as theory building
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article re-evaluates Peter Naur's 'Programming as Theory Building' in the context of AI agents, arguing that the engineer's core role is shifting from code writing to maintaining and verifying the system's mental model.
